\label{cor:massiverelativisticexistence}
  Let $d\in\mathbb{N}$, $\alpha\in(1,\min\{2,d\})$, and $\kappa\leq\kappa_{\rm c}$.
  Let $C_0\in\mathcal{K}_\alpha$ and assume in addition that, with $h(k):=C_0(k^2)$, $k>0$, the set $M_2:=\{k>0:\,h''(k)=(h'(k))^2\}$ has no accumulation point at zero.
  Let further $\tilde\kappa\leq\kappa$, and $V_\kappa:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be such that
  $$
  \frac{\tilde\kappa}{|x|^\alpha} \leq V_\kappa(x) \leq \frac{\kappa}{|x|^\alpha}, \quad x\in \mathbb{R}^d,
  $$
  and assume $V^S$ satisfies \eqref{eq:basicassumpshortrange} for some $\rho_S>1$. Then, the wave operators $W(C_0-V_\kappa,C_0)$, $W(C_0-V_\kappa-V^S,C_0-V_\kappa)$, and $W(C_0-V_\kappa-V^S,C_0)$ are asymptotically complete under the same assumptions as in Theorems~\ref{asympcomplhardy}(1) and~\ref{asympcomplhardyplusperturbation}(\ref{asympcomplhardyplusperturbation:acshortrange}).

body_md:
\label{giere}
  Let $H_0=P(D)$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, where $P:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is a real-valued, nonnegative, spherically symmetric Fourier multiplier, which is smooth away from the origin. Let $h(|\xi|):=P(\xi)$ and assume $h$ is nondecreasing with $h(k)\to\infty$ as $k\to\infty$.
  Assume further
  $$
  M_1 := \{ k>0:\, h'(k)=0\} \ \text{and}\ M_2 := \{ k>0:\, h''(k)=(h'(k))^2 \}
  $$
  are discrete in $\mathbb{R}_+$ with only possible accumulation point at infinity.
  Suppose Assumption~\ref{assumheatdifference} holds.  
  Then, the wave operators
  $$
  W(H,H_0)
  := \operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\infty}\mathrm{e}^{i t H}\mathrm{e}^{-i t H_0}P_{ac}(H_0)
  $$
  are asymptotically complete. Specifically, $\operatorname{ran}(W(H,H_0))=\mathcal{H}_{ac}(H)$ and $\mathcal{H}_{\rm sc}(H)=\{0\}$.

  \noindent
  (1) In \cite[Assumption~1.4]{Giere2004}, it is assumed that $S(t)-S_0(t)$ is compact for all $t\geq0$.
  However, it suffices to verify this assumption only for fixed $t_0>0$. Indeed, the compactness of $S(t_0)-S_0(t_0)$ for a fixed $t_0>0$ implies compactness of $S(t)-S_0(t)$ for every $t>0$. To see this, let $A:=S(t_0)$ and $A_0:=S_0(t_0)$, i.e., $\mathrm{e}^{-tH}=A^{t/t_0}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-tH_0}=A_0^{t/t_0}$. Since $\mathbb{R}_+\ni s\mapsto s^{t/t_0}$ is continuous, it follows from functional calculus that also $A^{t/t_0}-A_0^{t/t_0}$ is compact. The fact that Assumption~\ref{assumheatdifference} is only needed for fixed $t$ is also stated explicitly in \cite{Demuthetal2001}.

  \noindent
  (2) In this section, we use $P(\xi)=|\xi|^\alpha$. In this regard, we note that \cite[p.~133]{Giere2004} states that $P$ is assumed to be $C^\infty$, but inspection of the proof shows that only $P\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\})$ is used.

  \noindent

title: Proof
body_md:
By Trotter's formula,
  $$
  \mathrm{e}^{-tL_{\tilde\kappa}}(x,y) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-t(L_0-V_\kappa)}(x,y) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-tL_\kappa}(x,y)
  $$
  and therefore
  $$
  \left| S_V(t)(x,y) - S_0(t)(x,y) \right|
  \leq \left|S_\kappa(t)-S_0(t)\right| + \left|S_{\tilde\kappa}(t)-S_0(t)\right|.
  $$
  To conclude the proof, we apply Theorem~\ref{giere} by verifying Assumption~\ref{assumheatdifference}. We do so in the following two subsections, where we just consider $t=1$.
  To verify (ii), it suffices, by the above estimate, to consider the difference $S_\kappa-S_0$. To verify (i) for $\mathrm{e}^{-H}=S_V$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-H_0}=S_0$, we first verify it for $\mathrm{e}^{-H}=S_\kappa$ and then show how the compactness of $S_\kappa-S_0$ can be used to show compactness of $S_V-S_0$.
  Since our techniques make no use of the locality of $-\Delta$ or the Gaussian decay of heat kernels corresponding to the operators when $\alpha=2$, we will in the following only treat the case $0<\alpha<2$ explicitly. The generalizations to $\alpha=2$ are analogous.

label: eq:perturbedheatkernel
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H:=L_0-V_\kappa-V^S$. By the assumptions on $V_\kappa$ and Trotter's formula,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:perturbedheatkernel}
    \mathrm{e}^{-t (L_{\tilde \kappa}-V^S)}(x,y)
    \leq \mathrm{e}^{-tH}(x,y)
    \leq \mathrm{e}^{-t (L_\kappa-V^S)}(x,y).
  \end{align}
  Moreover,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:perturbedheatkernel2}
    0\leq \mathrm{e}^{-tH}(x,y) \leq \mathrm{e}^{t\|(V^S)_+\|_\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-tL_\kappa}(x,y).
  \end{align}
  We verify Assumption~\ref{assumheatdifference} with $H_0=L_0$.

  \smallskip
  \noindent
  {\bf On the boundedness assumption.}
  Choose $\gamma\in(1,\alpha\wedge\rho_S)$. By Duhamel's formula,
  $$
  \mathrm{e}^{-H}-\mathrm{e}^{-L_0} = \int_0^1 \mathrm{e}^{-(1-s)H}(V_\kappa+V^S)\mathrm{e}^{-sL_0}\,ds.
  $$
  Since $|V_\kappa(x)|\lesssim |x|^{-\alpha}$, the contribution containing $V_\kappa$ is bounded after composing from the right with $\langle \cdot\rangle^\gamma$ by the computations of Subsection~\ref{s:weightedbound} using \eqref{eq:perturbedheatkernel2}.

  For the contribution containing $V^S$, we use $\langle y\rangle^\gamma \lesssim \langle z\rangle^\gamma+|y-z|^\gamma$. Since $\gamma<\rho_S$, we have $\|V^S\langle z\rangle^\gamma\|_\infty<\infty$. Since $\gamma<\alpha$, we have
  $$
  \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}|z|^\gamma\mathrm{e}^{-sL_0}(z,0)\,dz \lesssim s^{\gamma/\alpha}.
  $$
  Hence,
  $$
  \|V^S\mathrm{e}^{-sL_0}\langle x\rangle^\gamma\| \lesssim 1+s^{\gamma/\alpha},
  \quad 0<s\leq1.
  $$
  Together with the $L^2$-boundedness of $\mathrm{e}^{-(1-s)H}$, this yields
  $$
  \|(\mathrm{e}^{-H}-\mathrm{e}^{-L_0})\langle x\rangle^\gamma\|<\infty.
  $$

  \smallskip
  \noindent
  {\bf On the compactness assumption.}
  By \eqref{eq:perturbedheatkernel2},
  $$
  |\mathrm{e}^{-H}(x,y)-\mathrm{e}^{-L_0}(x,y)| \lesssim \mathrm{e}^{-L_\kappa}(x,y)+\mathrm{e}^{-L_0}(x,y).
  $$
  Hence, the arguments of Subsection~\ref{s:compactness} extend to the present situation. Indeed, as before, we can check that $\chi_r(\mathrm{e}^{-H}-\mathrm{e}^{-L_0})$ is Hilbert--Schmidt. On the other hand, $\chi_r^c(\mathrm{e}^{-H}-\mathrm{e}^{-L_0})\chi_{r/2}$ tends to zero by the heat-kernel bounds and
  $$
  \|\chi_r^c(\mathrm{e}^{-H}-\mathrm{e}^{-L_0})\chi_{r/2}^c\| \lesssim r^{-\gamma}
  $$
  follows from the above-proved weighted estimate. Thus, $\mathrm{e}^{-H}-\mathrm{e}^{-L_0}$ is compact.

  \smallskip
  We can therefore apply Theorem~\ref{giere} and obtain the asymptotic completeness of $W(L_0-V_\kappa-V^S,L_0)$. By the chain rule and Theorem~\ref{asympcomplhardy}(1), we obtain also the asymptotic completeness of $W(L_0-V_\kappa-V^S,L_0-V_\kappa)$.

Let $E_H(\cdot)$ and $E_{H_0}(\cdot)$ denote the projection-valued spectral measures for $H$ and $H_0$, respectively.
  Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}$ be an arbitrary bounded Borel set. Thus, for any $t_0>0$, the operator $\mathrm{e}^{t_0 H} E_H(\Omega)$ is bounded on $\mathcal{H}$ and commutes with $H$. We factor
  $$
  A E_H(\Omega) = \left(A \mathrm{e}^{-t_0 H}\right)\cdot \left(\mathrm{e}^{t_0 H} E_H(\Omega)\right).
  $$
  By assumption, $A\mathrm{e}^{-t_0 H}$ is $H$-smooth. Thus, $A E_H(\Omega)$ is $H$-smooth as the product of an $H$-smooth operator and a bounded operator commuting with $H$. Since $\Omega$ is arbitrary, $A$ is locally $H$-smooth. The same argument also shows that $B$ is locally $H_0$-smooth. Thus, by local Kato smoothness theory \cite[Section~XIII.7]{ReedSimon1978}, it follows that $W(H,H_0)$ and $W(H_0,H)$ are asymptotically complete.

\label{rem:technicaldescription}
  The above proof is quite cumbersome. We first commuted $|D|^\beta$ out, then used the equivalence of Sobolev norms, only to commute $L_\kappa$ back to be next to $\mathrm{e}^{-t L_\kappa}$. The reason for doing so is that we do not know how to control $|D|^\beta\mathrm{e}^{-t L_\kappa}$. This leads to the technical assumption $s\leq 3\alpha/2$. (Note that a similar technical problem arises in \cite{Buietal2026}, where derivative bounds for heat kernels would also be beneficial.)
  The assumption $s>\alpha$ ensures that $[|D|^\alpha,|x|^s]$ is smoothing. As we explained above, this back-and-forth commuting is likely not necessary, hence also this assumption is likely technical, too.
   
  However, the assumption $\sigma<(d-\alpha)/2$ is not too surprising, because of the zero-energy resonance of $L_\kappa$, which is particularly severe when $\alpha\leq1$.

title: Remark
body_md:
One construction of an almost analytic extension of $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}:\,\mathbb{C})$ of order $N$ is
  $$
  \tilde f(z) := \left(\sum_{r=0}^N f^{(r)}(x)(iy)^r/r!\right) \eta\left(\frac{y}{\langle x\rangle}\right),
  $$
  where $\eta \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R};[0,1])$ satisfies $\eta(s)=1$ for $|s|\leq1$, $\eta(s)=0$ for $|s|>2$, and is smooth in between; see \cite{Davies1996,DimassiSjostrand1999}. The precise values of $N$ and choice of $\eta$ are not relevant.
  It is sometimes useful to indicate the order $N$ of the above construction, in which case we write more explicitly $\widetilde f_N(z)$ instead of just $\tilde f(z)$.
  Note that $\tilde f(z)$ is smooth as a function of $x$ and $y$, but not analytic, and that $\tilde f(z)|_\mathbb{R} = f(x)$. It follows from this construction that
  $$
  \left|\frac{\partial \tilde f}{\partial\overline z}\right|
  = \mathcal{O}(|\operatorname{Im}(z)|^N) \quad \text{as} \ y \to 0 \ \text{for all} \ x\in\mathbb{R}.
  $$
  In particular,
  $$
  \frac{\partial \tilde f}{\partial\overline z}=0, \quad z\in \mathbb{R},
  $$
  which is why one calls $\tilde f$ an almost analytic extension of $f$.
  The idea and above construction of almost analytic extensions was introduced by H\"ormander \cite[Section~4.2]{Hormander1969}. Further constructions were introduced by Mather \cite{Mather1971} and later by Jensen and Nakamura \cite{JensenNakamura1994}. See Sj\"ostrand's final comments in \cite{Hormander1969} and \cite[Ch.~8]{DimassiSjostrand1999} for more interesting historical remarks.
  It is also possible to prove \eqref{eq:hs} and formulae for higher-order derivatives $f^{(n)}(A)$ even if $f$ is not compactly supported, but decays at infinity. Such versions are contained, e.g., in \cite[Theorem~1.17, Corollary~1.18, Lemma~1.19]{Isozaki2023}.

label: eq:explicit-AA-extension
title: Proof
body_md:
Let us fix $N\in\{2,3,4,...\}$ and choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ such that
  $$
  \eta(s)=1 \quad \text{for} \ |s| \leq 1,
  \qquad
  \eta(s)=0 \quad \text{for} \ |s| \geq 2.
  $$
  We define the almost analytic extension
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:explicit-AA-extension}
    \widetilde f_N(x+iy)
    := \eta\left(\frac{y}{\langle x\rangle}\right) \sum_{k=0}^N \frac{f^{(k)}(x)(iy)^k}{k!},
  \end{align}
  which obeys
  $$
  \widetilde f_N|_{\mathbb{R}}=f, \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\widetilde f_N \subset \{x+iy:|y|\leq2\langle x\rangle\}.
  $$
  Moreover, by \eqref{eq:f-S0},
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:AA-extension-S0-corrected}
    |\overline\partial\widetilde f_N(x+iy)|
    \leq C_{f,N}\langle x\rangle^{-N-1}|y|^N \mathbf{1}_{|y|\leq2\langle x\rangle}.
  \end{align}
  Indeed, for those $x,y$ for which $\eta(y/\langle x\rangle)=1$, the terms of order strictly less than $N$ vanish when $\overline{\partial}$ is applied. On the other hand, on the support of the derivatives of $\eta$, we have $|y|\sim\langle x\rangle$. Thus, for $m\in\{2,3,...,N\}$, we obtain from \eqref{eq:AA-extension-S0-corrected},
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:Im-finite-corrected}
    \begin{split}
      \int_{\mathbb{C}} |\overline\partial\widetilde f_N(z)| |\operatorname{Im}(z)|^{-m}\,dx\,dy
      & \lesssim_{f,N} \int_{\mathbb{R}} \langle x\rangle^{-N-1} \int_0^{2\langle x\rangle} y^{N-m}\,dy\,dx \\
      & \lesssim \int_{\mathbb{R}}\langle x\rangle^{-m}\,dx < \infty.
    \end{split}
  \end{align}

  We next justify the Helffer--Sj\"ostrand commutator formula despite the fact that $f$ need not decay. Let $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ be such that
  $$
  \chi=1 \text{ on }[-1,1],
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\chi\subset[-2,2],
  $$
  and, for $L\geq1$, set
  $$
  f_L(x) := \chi(x/L)f(x).
  $$
  Then $f_L\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$,
  $$
  f_L(x) \to f(x) \quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}, \quad
  \sup_{L\geq1}\|f_L\|_\infty<\infty,
  $$
  and the family $(f_L)_{L\geq1}$ is bounded in $S^0(\mathbb{R})$; indeed,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:uniform-S0-truncations}
    \sup_{L\geq1}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} \langle x\rangle^k|f_L^{(k)}(x)|<\infty, \quad k\in\mathbb{N}_0.
  \end{align}
  Let $\widetilde f_{L,N}$ be defined from $f_L$ by the same construction as in \eqref{eq:explicit-AA-extension}. The estimate \eqref{eq:AA-extension-S0-corrected} then holds uniformly in $L$, and
  $$
  \overline{\partial} \widetilde f_{L,N}(z) \to \overline{\partial} \widetilde f_N(z)
  \quad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb{C}.
  $$
  Let
  $$
  B_t := \frac At \quad \text{and} \quad R_t(z):=(z-B_t)^{-1}.
  $$
  Since $B_t$ is selfadjoint,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:resolvent-bound}
    \|R_t(z)\| \leq |\operatorname{Im}(z)|^{-1}, \quad z\in\mathbb{C} \setminus \mathbb{R}.
  \end{align}
  Under the hypotheses of Item~(1), the resolvent commutator identity is
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:resolvent-commutator-first-corrected}
    [X,R_t(z)] = R_t(z)[X,B_t]R_t(z) = \frac1t R_t(z)[X,A]R_t(z).
  \end{align}
  To verify it, note that $R_t(z) \mathcal H \subset \mathcal{D}(A)$ and $X \mathcal{D}(A) \subset \mathcal{D}(A)$. Hence, all expressions are well-defined, initially on $\mathcal H$, and the identity follows from
  $$
  [X,T^{-1}] = -T^{-1}[X,T]T^{-1}, \quad T=z-B_t.
  $$
  Since $f_L$ is compactly supported, the usual Helffer--Sj\"ostrand formula in Proposition~\ref{prop:analyticextension} and \eqref{eq:resolvent-commutator-first-corrected} give
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:truncated-commutator-HS}
    [X,f_L(B_t)]
    = \frac{1}{2\pi i\,t} \int_{\mathbb{C}} \overline{\partial}\widetilde f_{L,N}(z) R_t(z) [X,A] R_t(z)\, dz\wedge d\overline z.
  \end{align}
  By the spectral theorem, $f_L(B_t) \to f(B_t)$ strongly, and hence
  $$
  [X,f_L(B_t)] \to [X,f(B_t)] \quad\text{strongly}.
  $$
  On the other hand, by \eqref{eq:resolvent-bound} and \eqref{eq:Im-finite-corrected} with $m=2$, dominated convergence shows that the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:truncated-commutator-HS} converges in operator norm. This shows \eqref{eq:first-commutator-HS-corrected} and
  \begin{align*}
    \|[X,f(B_t)]\|
    & \lesssim \frac1t \|[X,A]\| \int_{\mathbb{C}} |\overline\partial\widetilde f_N(z)| |\operatorname{Im}(z)|^{-2}\,dx\,dy
      \lesssim_f \frac1t\|[X,A]\|.
  \end{align*}
  This proves Item~(1).

  We now prove Item~(2), assuming $N\geq3$. Set
  $$
  C_t := [X,B_t]=\frac1t[X,A],
  \quad \text{and} \quad
  D_t := [C_t,B_t] = \frac1{t^2}[[X,A],A].
  $$
  Then,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:C-resolvent-corrected}
    [C_t,R_t(z)] = R_t(z)D_tR_t(z).
  \end{align}
  Thus, $C_t R_t(z) = R_t(z)C_t+R_t(z)D_tR_t(z)$, and therefore
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:resolvent-second-expansion-corrected}
    R_t(z)C_tR_t(z) = R_t(z)^2C_t+R_t(z)^2D_tR_t(z).
  \end{align}
  Substituting this into \eqref{eq:first-commutator-HS-corrected} yields
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:second-commutator-HS-corrected}
    \begin{split}
      [X,f(B_t)]
      & = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \left(\int_{\mathbb{C}} \overline{\partial}\widetilde f_N(z) R_t(z)^2 \,dz \wedge d\overline z\right) C_t \\
      & \quad + \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\mathbb{C}} \overline{\partial}\widetilde f_N(z) R_t(z)^2D_tR_t(z)\, dz \wedge d\overline z.
    \end{split}
  \end{align}
  It remains to identify the first integral. For every $L\geq1$, differentiation of the scalar Helffer--Sj\"ostrand formula for $f_L=\chi(\cdot/L)f$ gives
  $$
  f_L'(B_t)
  = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\mathbb{C}} \overline{\partial}\widetilde f_{L,N}(z) R_t(z)^2 \,dz \wedge d\overline z.
  $$
  We have
  $$
  f_L'(x)-f'(x) = (\chi(x/L)-1)f'(x) + \frac1L\chi'(x/L)f(x),
  $$
  and therefore
  $$
  \|f_L'-f'\|_\infty \lesssim_f L^{-1}.
  $$
  Hence, $f_L'(B_t)\to f'(B_t)$ in operator norm. Applying dominated convergence once more, using $m=2$ in \eqref{eq:Im-finite-corrected} yields
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:derivative-HS-corrected}
    f'(B_t) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\mathbb{C}} \overline{\partial}\widetilde f_N(z) R_t(z)^2 \,dz\wedge d\overline z.
  \end{align}
  Thus, the first term in \eqref{eq:second-commutator-HS-corrected} equals
  $$
  f'(B_t)C_t = \frac1t f'(B_t)[X,A].
  $$
  Since $D_t=t^{-2}[[X,A],A]$, the second term is
  $$
  \mathcal{E}_f(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi i\,t^2} \int_{\mathbb{C}} \overline{\partial}\widetilde f_N(z) R_t(z)^2[[X,A],A]R_t(z)\, dz\wedge d\overline z.
  $$
  Finally,
  $$
  \|R_t(z)^2[[X,A],A]R_t(z)\| \leq |\operatorname{Im}(z)|^{-3} \|[[X,A],A]\|.
  $$
  Therefore, by \eqref{eq:Im-finite-corrected} with $m=3$,
  \begin{align*}
    \|\mathcal{E}_f(t)\|
    & \lesssim \frac1{t^2} \|[[X,A],A]\| \int_{\mathbb{C}} |\overline{\partial}\widetilde f_N(z)| |\operatorname{Im}(z)|^{-3}\,dx\,dy \\
    & \lesssim_f \frac1{t^2}\|[[X,A],A]\|.
  \end{align*}
  This proves Item~(2).

\label{rem:Lkappa-ac-spectrum}
  Let us recall the argument showing that $\sigma(L_\kappa)=\sigma_{\rm ac}(L_\kappa)=[0,\infty)$ for $\kappa<\kappa_{\rm c}$.
  First, since $\kappa<\kappa_{\rm c}$, we have, by Hardy's inequality, $L_\kappa\gtrsim|D|^\alpha\geq0$. Thus, zero cannot be an eigenvalue. (In fact, zero is also not an eigenvalue for $\kappa=\kappa_{\rm c}$ as a consequence of the ground state representation of $L_\kappa$, stated, e.g., in \cite[Proposition~4.1]{Franketal2008H}.) Moreover, Lemma~\ref{lem5} and the separability of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ exclude positive eigenvalues. Finally, on every compact interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$,
  $$
  E_I(L_\kappa)i[L_\kappa,A]E_I(L_\kappa) = \alpha E_I(L_\kappa)L_\kappa E_I(L_\kappa) \geq \alpha\inf(I)E_I(L_\kappa),
  $$
  and Mourre theory (see, e.g., \cite[Corollary~1.51]{Isozaki2023}) excludes singular continuous spectrum on $(0,\infty)$.

First notice that $\chi$ satisfies the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{lem:functional-calculus-commutator}.

  Let us prove \eqref{eq:chi-VL-commutator}. By assumption, $V,x\cdot\nabla V \in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Multiplication by $V$ preserves $\mathcal D(A)$ and, on $\mathcal{D}(A)$, we have $[V,A]=i\,x\cdot\nabla V$. Hence, $V\in C^1(A)$ and, for $t\geq1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:functional-calculus-commutator} yields
  $$
  \|[\chi(A/t),V]\| \lesssim_\chi t^{-1}\|x\cdot\nabla V\|_\infty \lesssim t^{-1}.
  $$
  For $0<t<1$,
  $$
  \|[\chi(A/t),V]\| \leq2\|\chi\|_\infty \|V\|_\infty.
  $$
  This proves \eqref{eq:chi-VL-commutator}.

  We turn to \eqref{eq:chi-resolvent-commutator}. Set
  $$
  B := i[H,A].
  $$
  We first verify that $R_\lambda\in C^1(A)$. Let $U(s):=\mathrm{e}^{isA}$ for $s\in\mathbb{R}$. By the dilation covariance of $L_\kappa$ (Lemma~\ref{lem5}), we have $U(s)L_\kappa U(-s) = \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha s}L_\kappa$. Moreover, $U(s)VU(-s)=V(\mathrm{e}^{s}x)$. Hence, with $H_s:=U(s)HU(-s)$, we have $H_s=\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha s}L_\kappa-V(\mathrm{e}^{s} x)$. Since $V$ is bounded, $\mathcal D(H)=\mathcal D(L_\kappa)$, and this domain is invariant under $U(s)$. Set $F(x):=x\cdot\nabla V(x)$. By~\eqref{ass5}, $x\cdot\nabla F\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Moreover, for $s\neq0$
  $$
  \frac{V(\mathrm{e}^{s} x)-V(x)}{s} = \int_0^1F(e^{\theta s}x)\,d\theta.
  $$
  Since $\|F(\mathrm{e}^{s}\cdot) - F\|_\infty \leq |s|\,\|x\cdot\nabla F\|_\infty$,
  $$
  \lim_{s\to0}\frac{V(\mathrm{e}^{s}\cdot)-V}{s} = F \quad\text{in }L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d).
  $$
  Thus,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:H-dilation-derivative}
    \lim_{s\to0} \frac{H_s-H}{s} = -\alpha L_\kappa-x\cdot\nabla V = -B \quad\text{in }\mathcal B(\mathcal D(H),L^2)
  \end{align}
  where $\mathcal D(H)$ is equipped with the graph norm. Let
  $$
  R_{\lambda,s} := U(s)R_\lambda U(-s) = (\lambda+H_s)^{-1}.
  $$
  Since $H_s$ is unitarily equivalent to $H$, we have $\|R_{\lambda,s}\| = \|R_\lambda\| \leq\delta^{-1}$. Using
  $$
  \frac{R_{\lambda,s}-R_\lambda}{s} = -R_{\lambda,s} \frac{H_s-H}{s} R_\lambda
  $$
  and \eqref{eq:H-dilation-derivative}, we obtain
  $$
  \lim_{s\to0}\frac{R_{\lambda,s}-R_\lambda}{s} = R_\lambda B R_\lambda \quad\text{in }\mathcal B(L^2).
  $$
  Thus, $R_\lambda\in C^1(A)$. In particular,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:resolvent-A-commutator}
    R_\lambda\mathcal D(A)\subset\mathcal D(A),
    \qquad
    [R_\lambda,A] = iR_\lambda B R_\lambda.
  \end{align}
  By Lemma~\ref{lem5},
  $$
  B = i[H,A] = \alpha L_\kappa+x\cdot\nabla V = \alpha H+W,
  $$
  where $W:=\alpha V+x\cdot\nabla V \in\mathcal B(L^2)$. Therefore,
  $$
  R_\lambda B R_\lambda = \alpha(R_\lambda-\lambda R_\lambda^2) + R_\lambda W R_\lambda \in\mathcal B(L^2).
  $$
  Hence, $[R_\lambda,A]\in\mathcal B(L^2)$. Thus, for $t\geq1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:functional-calculus-commutator} yields
  $$
  \|[\chi(A/t),R_\lambda]\| \lesssim_\chi t^{-1}\|[R_\lambda,A]\| \lesssim_{\delta,V} t^{-1}.
  $$
  Finally, for $0<t<1$,
  $$
  \|[\chi(A/t),R_\lambda]\| \leq 2\|\chi\|_\infty\|R_\lambda\| \lesssim t^{-1}.
  $$
  This proves \eqref{eq:chi-resolvent-commutator}.

\label{lem:fractional-A-commutator}

  [B,A] = BA-AB,
  \qquad
  \mathcal D([B,A])=\mathcal D(A),
  $$
  extends to a bounded operator on $\mathcal H$.

  $$
  B\mathcal D(\langle A\rangle^s) \subset \mathcal D(\langle A\rangle^s)
  $$
  and $[B,\langle A\rangle^s]$, initially defined on $\mathcal{D}(\langle A\rangle^s)$, extends to a bounded operator on $\mathcal H$ with
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:fractional-A-abstract-comm-bound}
    \|[B,\langle A\rangle^s]\| \lesssim_s \|[B,A]\|.

label: eq:fractional-AA-symbol
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $f(x) := \langle x\rangle^s$. Then $f\in S^s(\mathbb{R})$, i.e.,
  $$
  |f^{(k)}(x)| \lesssim_{s,k} \langle x\rangle^{s-k}, \quad k\in\mathbb{N}_0.
  $$
  Choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ such that
  $$
  \eta(r)=1\quad\text{for }|r|\leq1,
  \qquad
  \eta(r)=0\quad\text{for }|r|\geq2,
  $$
  and, for $N\in\{2,3,...\}$, define the almost analytic extension
  $$
  \widetilde f_N(x+iy) := \eta\left(\frac{y}{\langle x\rangle}\right) \sum_{k=0}^N \frac{f^{(k)}(x)(iy)^k}{k!}.
  $$
  Then,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:fractional-AA-symbol}
    |\overline\partial\widetilde f_N(x+iy)|
    \lesssim_{s,N} \langle x\rangle^{s-N-1}|y|^N \mathbf{1}_{|y|\leq2\langle x\rangle}.
  \end{align}
  Thus,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:fractional-AA-integrability}
    \int_{\mathbb{C}} |\overline\partial\widetilde f_N(z)| |\operatorname{Im} z|^{-2}\,dx\,dy 
    \lesssim \int_{\mathbb{R}} \langle x\rangle^{s-N-1} \int_0^{2\langle x\rangle} y^{N-2}\,dy\,dx
    \lesssim \int_{\mathbb{R}}\langle x\rangle^{s-2}\,dx
    < \infty
  \end{align}
  since $s<1$. As in Lemma~\ref{lem:functional-calculus-commutator}, we can represent $[B,f(A)]$ as a Helffer--Sj\"ostrand-type integral by a truncation argument. To this end, let $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ be such that
  $$
  0\leq\chi\leq1,\qquad
  \chi=1\ \text{on }[-1,1],\qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\chi\subset[-2,2],
  $$
  and set
  $$
  f_L(x):=\chi(x/L)f(x), \quad L\geq1.
  $$
  Then $f_L\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, and $(f_L)_{L\geq1}$ is bounded in $S^s(\mathbb{R})$, uniformly in $L$. Let $\widetilde f_{L,N}$ be the corresponding almost analytic extensions. Since $f_L$ is compactly supported, the ordinary Helffer--Sj\"ostrand formula yields
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:fractional-truncated-comm}
    [B,f_L(A)] = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\mathbb{C}} \overline\partial\widetilde f_{L,N}(z) (z-A)^{-1}[B,A](z-A)^{-1} \,dz\wedge d\overline z.
  \end{align}
  Hence, by $\|(z-A)^{-1}\|\leq|\operatorname{Im} z|^{-1}$, \eqref{eq:fractional-AA-integrability}, and dominated convergence, the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:fractional-truncated-comm} converges in operator norm as $L\to\infty$ to a bounded operator $K$ satisfying
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:fractional-K-bound}
    \|K\| \lesssim_s \|[B,A]\|.
  \end{align}

  It remains to identify $K$ with $[B,\langle A\rangle^s]$ and show the domain invariance. Let $u\in\mathcal D(\langle A\rangle^s)$. By the spectral theorem,
  $$
  f_L(A)u \to f(A)u = \langle A\rangle^s u \quad \text{as } L\to\infty.
  $$
  Moreover,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:fractional-domain-limit}
    f_L(A)Bu = Bf_L(A)u-[B,f_L(A)]u.
  \end{align}
  The right-hand side converges in $\mathcal H$. In particular,
  $$
  \sup_{L\geq1}\|f_L(A)Bu\|<\infty.
  $$
  Since $f_L(x)\to f(x)$ pointwise, Fatou's lemma applied to the measure $\langle Bu,dE_A(\cdot)Bu\rangle$ yields
  $$
  \int_\mathbb{R} |f(\lambda)|^2\, \langle Bu,dE_A(\lambda)Bu\rangle < \infty.
  $$
  Hence, $Bu\in\mathcal D(f(A)) = \mathcal D(\langle A\rangle^s)$ and by the spectral theorem,
  $$
  f_L(A)Bu \to f(A)Bu \quad \text{as }L\to\infty.
  $$
  Taking the limit in \eqref{eq:fractional-domain-limit} shows
  $$
  B\langle A\rangle^s u - \langle A\rangle^s Bu = Ku.
  $$
  Therefore,
  $$
  [B,\langle A\rangle^s]=K
  $$
  on $\mathcal D(\langle A\rangle^s)$, and \eqref{eq:fractional-A-abstract-comm-bound} follows from \eqref{eq:fractional-K-bound}.

\label{assumskibsted}

Assume also the following statements.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item With ${\rm ad}_{A(\tau)}^{0}(H)=H$ and $1 \leq n \leq n_0$, the (commutator-)form (defined iteratively) $i^n{\rm ad}_{A(\tau)}^n(H)$ on $\mathcal{D}(H)\cap\mathcal{D}$ extends to a symmetric operator with domain $\mathcal{D}(H)$.

  \item If $A$ is unbounded, then $\sup_{|s|<1}\|H\mathrm{e}^{i A(\tau)s}\psi\|<\infty$ for all $\psi\in\mathcal{D}(H)$ and $\tau \geq t_0$.

  \item For any $\tau_1,\tau_2 \geq t_0$, $A(\tau_1)-A(\tau_2)$ is bounded, and the derivative $d_{\tau}A(\tau) = \frac{d}{d\tau} A(\tau)$ exists as a bounded operator.

    For $n \leq n_0-1$ and $\tau \geq t_0$ the form (defined iteratively)
    $$
    i^n {\rm ad}_{A(\tau)}^{n}(d_\tau A(\tau)) = i [i^{n-1}{\rm ad}_{A(\tau)}^{n-1}(d_\tau A(\tau)),A(\tau)]
    $$
    on $\mathcal{D}$ extends to a bounded selfadjoint operator on $\mathcal{H}$.

  \item For $n\leq n_0$, ${\rm ad}_{A(\tau)}^{n}(H) (H-i)^{-1}$ and ${\rm ad}_{A(\tau)}^{n-1}(d_\tau A(\tau))$ are continuous, $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$-valued functions of $\tau \geq t_0$.

  \item
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] ${\rm ad}_{A(\tau)}^{n_0-1}(d_\tau A(\tau)) = \mathcal{O}(\tau^{k_0})$ in $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ as $\tau\to\infty$.

    \item[(b)] For $n\leq n_0$, we have ${\rm ad}_{A(\tau)}^{n-1}(d_\tau A(\tau))(H-i)^{-1} = \mathcal{O}(1)$ in $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ as $\tau\to\infty$.

    \item[(c)] For $n\leq n_0$, we have ${\rm ad}_{A(\tau)}^{n}(H)(H-i)^{-1} = \mathcal{O}(1)$ in $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ as $\tau\to\infty$.
    \end{enumerate}

  \item The statement $q(\beta_0,\alpha_0)$, defined as follows, holds:

    With $\alpha_0'=\max\{m\in\mathbb{N}:\,m<\alpha_0\}$ (for $\alpha_0>1$) the following (positivity) estimate holds for $(\beta,\alpha)=(0,1),...,(0,\alpha_0'),(\beta_0,\alpha_0)$(=$(\beta_0,\alpha_0)$ if $0<\alpha_0\leq1$):

    Let $\mathbb D_HA(\tau)$ denote the symmetric operator $i[H,A(\tau)] + d_\tau A(\tau)$, the Heisenberg derivative. Given $\varepsilon>0$ and $g(x,\tau)\in \mathcal{F}_{\beta,\alpha,\varepsilon}$, there is $C>0$ so that with
    $$
    \zeta(t) = (g^{(1)}(A(\tau),\tau))^{1/2}\mathrm{e}^{-i t H}f(H)B^{-\alpha/2}\varphi,

    \int_0^\infty dt \left(\langle \zeta(t), f_2(H) \mathbb D_H A(\tau) f_2(H)\zeta(t)\rangle\right)_-
    \leq C \|\varphi\|^2, \qquad \varphi\in\mathcal{H}.
    $$
  \end{enumerate}

body_md:
\label{the11suff-unified}
  Let $d\in\mathbb{N}$, $\alpha\in(1/2,2]\cap(1/2,d)$, and $\kappa<\kappa_{\rm c}$.
  Assume $V^S$ satisfies \eqref{eq:basicassumpshortrange} and \eqref{ass5} for some $\rho_S>1$. Let $\sigma = \Phi^{-1}(\kappa)<(d-1)/2$ if $\alpha\leq1$ and $H_\kappa=L_\kappa-V^S$.
  Let
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:mu-unified}
    1 < \mu < \min\{\rho_S,2,2\alpha,d-2\sigma\},
  \end{align}
  $$
  K_0,K_1 \in \{L_\kappa,H_\kappa\},
  $$
  and $f_0,f_1\in C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$ be real-valued.
  Let $\theta>0$, and choose a nondecreasing $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R};[0,1])$ such that
  $$
  \chi(s)=0\quad \text{for} \ s\leq\theta/4,
  \qquad
  \chi(s)=1\quad \text{for} \ s\geq\theta/2.
  $$
  Then
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:unified-localized-Cook}
    \left\| f_1(K_1)\mathrm{e}^{itK_1} V^S \chi\left(\frac At\right)^2 \mathrm{e}^{-itK_0}f_0(K_0) \right\|
    \lesssim_{f_0,f_1} t^{-\mu}, \quad t\geq1.
  \end{align}

label: eq:unified-spectral-regularity
title: Proof
body_md:
We first verify that
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:unified-spectral-regularity}
    \langle D\rangle^{\mu/2}f_j(K_j) \in\mathcal B(L^2), \qquad j\in\{0,1\}.
  \end{align}
  Since $\mu/\alpha<2$ and $\mu<d-2\sigma$, Proposition~\ref{eqsob} yields
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:unified-Sobolev}
    \| |D|^{\mu/2}u \| \lesssim \|L_\kappa^{\mu/(2\alpha)} u\|.
  \end{align}
  If $K_j=L_\kappa$, then
  $$
  L_\kappa^{\mu/(2\alpha)} f_j(L_\kappa) \in\mathcal B(L^2)
  $$
  by the spectral theorem. If $K_j=H_\kappa$, then by the boundedness of $V^S$, we have $\mathcal{D}(H_\kappa) = \mathcal{D}(L_\kappa)$ with equivalent graph norms. In particular,
  $$
  L_\kappa f_j(H_\kappa)
  = H_\kappa f_j(H_\kappa) + V^S f_j(H_\kappa) \in \mathcal B(L^2).
  $$
  Interpolation for the nonnegative selfadjoint operator $L_\kappa$ therefore gives
  $$
  L_\kappa^{\mu/(2\alpha)} f_j(H_\kappa) \in \mathcal B(L^2).
  $$
  Together with \eqref{eq:unified-Sobolev}, this proves \eqref{eq:unified-spectral-regularity}. Let
  $$
  w(x) = \langle x\rangle^{-\mu/2}.
  $$
  By Lemma~\ref{lem12},
  $$
  Q_\mu := \langle D\rangle^{-\mu/2} w\langle A\rangle^\mu w \langle D\rangle^{-\mu/2}
  $$
  is bounded. Hence, \eqref{eq:unified-spectral-regularity} implies
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:unified-weighted-A}
    f_j(K_j)w\langle A\rangle^\mu wf_j(K_j) \in\mathcal B(L^2),
    \qquad j\in\{0,1\}.
  \end{align}
  We next claim that, if $\eta\in S^0(\mathbb{R})$ with $\operatorname{supp}\eta\subset[c,\infty)$ for some $c>0$, then
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:unified-weighted-outgoing}
    \left\| w\eta\left(\frac At\right) \mathrm{e}^{-itK_j}f_j(K_j) \right\|
    \lesssim_{\eta,f_j} t^{-\mu/2}, \qquad t\geq1.
  \end{align}
  Indeed, functional calculus for $A$ gives
  $$
  \eta\left(\frac At\right)^* \eta\left(\frac At\right)
  \lesssim t^{-\mu}\langle A\rangle^\mu.
  $$
  Thus, for
  $$
  u_{j,t} = \mathrm{e}^{-itK_j} f_j(K_j)u, \quad u \in L^2
  $$
  estimate \eqref{eq:unified-weighted-A} yields
  $$
  \left\| \eta\left(\frac At\right)w u_{j,t} \right\|
  \lesssim_{f_j} t^{-\mu/2} \|u\|.
  $$
  Moreover, since $[w,A]=i\, x\cdot\nabla w$ is bounded, by Lemma~\ref{lem:functional-calculus-commutator}(1) with $X=w$ and $f=\eta$ (with $\eta\in C^\infty$ bounded and $\eta'$ compactly supported), we have
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:unified-commutator-w-eta}
    \left\| \left[w,\eta\left(\frac At\right)\right] \right\| \lesssim_\eta t^{-1}.
  \end{align}
  Since $\mu<2$, we have $t^{-1}\lesssim t^{-\mu/2}$ for $t\geq1$. Therefore,
  \begin{align*}
    \left\| w\eta\left(\frac At\right)u_{j,t} \right\|
    & \leq \left\| \eta\left(\frac At\right)wu_{j,t} \right\| + \left\| \left[w,\eta\left(\frac At\right)\right]u_{j,t} \right\|
      \lesssim_{\eta,f_j} t^{-\mu/2} \|u\|,
  \end{align*}
  which proves \eqref{eq:unified-weighted-outgoing}.

  Let $u,v\in L^2$ and
  $$
  \chi_t=\chi(A/t),
  \qquad
  u_t = \mathrm{e}^{-itK_0}f_0(K_0)u,
  \qquad
  v_t = \mathrm{e}^{-itK_1}f_1(K_1)v.
  $$
  We have
  $$
  V^S\chi_t^2 = \chi_tV^S\chi_t+[V^S,\chi_t]\chi_t.
  $$
  Since $\mu<\rho_S$,
  $$
  |V^S(x)| \lesssim w(x)^2.
  $$
  Therefore, by \eqref{eq:unified-weighted-outgoing},
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:unified-main-term}
    \left| \langle v_t, \chi_t V^S \chi_t u_t\rangle \right|
    = \left| \langle \chi_t v_t, V^S\chi_tu_t\rangle \right|
    \lesssim \| w \chi_t u_t \| \, \| w \chi_t v_t\|
    \lesssim_{f_0,f_1} t^{-\mu} \|u\| \|v\|.
  \end{align}
  It remains to estimate the $[V^S,\chi_t]\chi_t$ term. By Lemma~\ref{lem:functional-calculus-commutator}(2) with $X=V^S$ and $f=\chi$ (whose assumptions are satisfied since $x\cdot\nabla V^S, x\cdot\nabla(x\cdot\nabla V^S) \in L^\infty$),
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:unified-commutator-expansion}
    [V^S,\chi_t] = \frac1t\chi'\left(\frac At\right)[V^S,A] + \mathcal{E}_t,
    \qquad
    \|\mathcal{E}_t\| \lesssim t^{-2}
  \end{align}
  with
  \begin{align*}
    \mathcal{E}_t = \frac{1}{2\pi i t^2} \int_\mathbb{C} \overline{\partial}\tilde\chi(z) \left(z-\frac At\right)^{-2} \, [[V^S,A],A]\, \left(z-\frac{A}{t}\right)^{-1}\,dz \wedge d\overline{z},
  \end{align*}
  which indeed obeys $\|\mathcal{E}_t\| \lesssim t^{-2} \|(x\cdot \nabla)^2 V^S\|_\infty$. Here, we have used that $[V^S,A] = i \, x\cdot\nabla V^S$ and $[[V^S,A],A] = -(x\cdot\nabla)^2 V^S$ are bounded.
  Since $\chi,\chi'\in S^0(\mathbb{R})$ and are supported in a positive half-line and we have $|[V^S,A](x)| \lesssim \langle x\rangle^{-\rho_S} \lesssim w(x)^2$, \eqref{eq:unified-weighted-outgoing} gives
  \begin{align*}
    \left| \left\langle v_t, \chi'\left(\frac At\right) [V^S,A]\chi_tu_t \right\rangle \right|
    & \lesssim \|w \chi_t u_t\| \, \left\| w \chi'\left(\frac At\right) v_t \right\| 
      \lesssim_{f_0,f_1} t^{-\mu} \|u\| \|v\|.
  \end{align*}
  It follows from \eqref{eq:unified-commutator-expansion} that
  $$
  \left| \langle[V^S,\chi_t]\chi_tu_t,v_t\rangle \right|
  \lesssim_{f_0,f_1} (t^{-1-\mu}+t^{-2}) \|u\| \|v\|
  \lesssim t^{-\mu}\|u\| \|v\|
  $$
  since $1<\mu<2$. Combining this with \eqref{eq:unified-main-term} proves \eqref{eq:unified-localized-Cook}.

  Recall $H_0=L_\kappa$ has purely absolutely continuous spectrum $[0,\infty)$ (Remark~\ref{rem:Lkappa-ac-spectrum}). Moreover, since $V^S$ is bounded and decays, $V^S$ is relatively compact with respect to $L_0$ and, since $H_0$ has the same form domain as $L_0$, also with respect to $H_0=L_\kappa$. Hence, Weyl's theorem for the essential spectrum $\sigma_{\rm ess}(H)$ of $H$ implies $\sigma_{\rm ess}(H)=[0,\infty)$, and the spectrum of $H$ in $(-\infty,0)$ is discrete. Moreover, the Mourre estimate \eqref{eq:the6-local-strict-mourre} used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{the6}, together with $H\in C^2(A)$, implies absence of singular continuous spectrum on $(0,\infty)$ and local finiteness of the positive eigenvalues away from zero. Hence,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:proof-acshortrangesmallalpha-b-no-sc}
    \mathcal H_{\rm sc}(H) = \{0\}.
  \end{align}
  Let $f_0\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb{R})$ be such that $\operatorname{supp} f_0 \cap \sigma_{\rm p}(K)=\emptyset$ with $K\in\{H_0,H\}$. Choose $f_1\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb{R})$ such that $f_1=1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp} f_0$.  
  Thus, Theorem~\ref{the6} with $f\equiv f_0$ there is applicable. Let $\theta>0$ and $T>0$ be the resulting constants.
  By the assumptions $1/2<\alpha\leq1$, $\sigma<(d-1)/2$, and $\rho_S>1$, we may choose
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:proof-acshortrangesmallalpha-b-mu}
    1 < \mu < \min\{\rho_S,2,2\alpha,d-2\sigma\}.
  \end{align}  
  With this choice, Lemma~\ref{the11suff-unified} is applicable.

  \medskip
  \noindent
  {\bf Step 2: Existence of $W(H,H_0)$.}
  Let $f_0\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb{R})$ and $f_1\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb{R})$ be such that $f_1=1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp} f_0$. Consider
  $$
  U_{10}(t) := f_1(H) \mathrm{e}^{itH} \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0} f_0(H_0)
  $$
  and fix $\nu>1$. Since $H-H_0=-V^S$,
  $$
  \frac{d}{dt}U_{10}(t) = -i f_1(H) \mathrm{e}^{itH} V^S \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}f_0(H_0).
  $$
  Then, Lemma~\ref{the11suff-unified}, with $K_1=H$ and $K_0=H_0$, yields
  $$
  \left\| f_1(H) \mathrm{e}^{itH} V^S\chi_t^2 \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}f_0(H_0) \right\|
  \lesssim_{f_0,f_1,T} t^{-\mu}, \quad t\geq T.
  $$
  By \eqref{eq:proof-acshortrangesmallalpha-b-cutoff} and Theorem~\ref{the6},
  \begin{align*}
    \left\| f_1(H) \mathrm{e}^{itH} V^S (1-\chi_t^2) \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}f_0(H_0)\varphi \right\| 
    & \lesssim \left\| F_t f_0(H_0) \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}\varphi \right\| \\
    & \lesssim_{f_0,\nu,T} t^{-\nu} \|\langle A\rangle^\nu \varphi \|, \quad t\geq T, \ \varphi \in \mathcal{D}(\langle A\rangle^\nu).
  \end{align*}
  Since $\mu,\nu>1$, the derivative $\frac{d}{dt}U_{10}(t)\varphi$ is integrable on $[T,\infty)$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\langle A\rangle^\nu)$. Hence, $U_{10}(t)\varphi$ has a limit on this dense subspace. As $\sup_{t\geq T}\|U_{10}(t)\| \leq \|f_1\|_\infty\|f_0\|_\infty$, this strong limit extends to all of $L^2$.

  Since $V^S$ is relatively compact with respect to $H_0$,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:proof-acshortrangesmallalpha-b-compact-fc}
    h(H)-h(H_0) \ \text{is compact for all} \ h\in C_0(\mathbb{R}).
  \end{align}
  Since $(1-f_1)f_0=0$,
  \begin{align*}
    (1-f_1(H)) \mathrm{e}^{itH} \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}f_0(H_0)
    = \mathrm{e}^{itH} (1-f_1(H)) (f_0(H_0)-f_0(H)) \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}.
  \end{align*}
  By \eqref{eq:proof-acshortrangesmallalpha-b-compact-fc}, $f_0(H_0)-f_0(H)$ is compact.
  Moreover, $\mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}\varphi\rightharpoonup0$ as $t\to\infty$ since $H_0$ has purely absolutely continuous spectrum; here $\rightharpoonup$ denotes weak convergence. Thus,
  $
  \operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\infty}(1-f_1(H)) \mathrm{e}^{itH} \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}f_0(H_0)=0.
  $
  Therefore, $\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\infty} \mathrm{e}^{itH} \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}f_0(H_0)$ exists.


  Since $H_0$ has purely absolutely continuous spectrum $[0,\infty)$, the union of the ranges of $f_0(H_0)$ is dense in $L^2$. Since $\mathrm{e}^{i t H} \mathrm{e}^{-i t H_0}$ are unitary (hence uniformly bounded in $t$), we obtain the existence of $W(H,H_0)$.


  \medskip
  \noindent
  {\bf Step 3: Existence of $W(H_0,H)$.}
  Let $f_0\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb{R})$ and satisfy $\operatorname{supp} f_0\cap\sigma_{\rm p}(H)=\emptyset$. Choose $f_1\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb{R})$ such that $f_1=1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp} f_0$.
  Fix $\nu>1$ and let
  $$
  \widetilde U_{10}(t) := f_1(H_0) \mathrm{e}^{itH_0} \mathrm{e}^{-itH} f_0(H).
  $$
  By exactly the same arguments that showed the existence of $\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\infty}\mathrm{e}^{itH}\mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}f_0(H_0)$, we obtain the existence of $\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\infty} \mathrm{e}^{itH_0}\mathrm{e}^{-itH}f_0(H)$. It remains to replace $f_0(H)$ with $P_{\rm ac}(H)$. We proceed similarly as before. First note that the union of the ranges of the operators $f_0(H)$ is dense in $\mathcal H_{\rm ac}(H)$; indeed, the negative spectrum is discrete, hence carries no absolutely continuous part. Moreover, $E_H(\{0\})P_{\rm ac}(H)=0$, i.e., the absolutely continuous subspace is exhausted by compact positive-energy intervals away from zero. On any interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, there are only finitely many eigenvalues of $H$. Since an absolutely continuous spectral measure gives zero mass to those points, one can choose smooth compactly supported functions $f_0$ whose supports avoid those eigenvalues and which approximate $1$ on $[a,b]$ except in arbitrarily small neighborhoods of them. Thus,
  $$
  \overline{\bigcup_{f_0\in C_c^\infty(0,\infty),\,\operatorname{supp}(f_0)\cap\sigma_{\rm p}(H)=\emptyset}\operatorname{ran}(f_0(H))} = \mathcal H_{\rm ac}(H).
  $$
  Hence, $W(H_0,H)=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\infty}\mathrm{e}^{itH_0}\mathrm{e}^{-itH}P_{\rm ac}(H)$ exists.

  \medskip
  \noindent
  {\bf Step 4: Conclusion.}
  Passing to the strong limit in $\left( \mathrm{e}^{itH} \mathrm{e}^{-itH_0}\right) \left(\mathrm{e}^{itH_0} \mathrm{e}^{-itH}P_{\rm ac}(H)\right) = P_{\rm ac}(H)$ yields $W(H,H_0)W(H_0,H)=P_{\rm ac}(H)$. Since $\operatorname{ran} W(H,H_0) \subset\mathcal H_{\rm ac}(H)$, the preceding identity gives the reverse inclusion. Therefore, $\operatorname{ran} W(H,H_0) = \mathcal H_{\rm ac}(H)$. Thus, $W(L_\kappa-V^S,L_\kappa)$ is asymptotically complete.

title: Proof
body_md:
We treat both statements simultaneously.
  Let $0<\alpha\leq1$, $\kappa\neq0$, and
  $$
  T_0=
  \begin{cases}
    L_0=(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2},\\
    C_0=C_0(-\Delta),
  \end{cases}
  \qquad
  T_\kappa := T_0-\frac{\kappa}{|x|^\alpha}.
  $$
  We aim to apply Lemma~\ref{lem:generalized-ishida-wada} with
  $$
  H_0 = T_0,
  \qquad
  U(x) = \frac{\kappa}{|x|^\alpha},
  \qquad
  H = T_\kappa.
  $$
  For $T_0=L_0$, the Fourier symbol is
  $$
  p(\xi)=|\xi|^\alpha = \Psi(|\xi|^2),
  \qquad
  \Psi(\lambda)=\lambda^{\alpha/2}
  $$
  with $\Psi'(\lambda)>0$ for all $\lambda>0$.
  For $T_0=C_0$, the defining properties of $\mathcal{K}_\alpha$ imply that $C_0$ is a nonconstant Bernstein function. Hence, $C_0\in C^\infty(0,\infty)$ and $C_0'(\lambda)>0$ for all $\lambda>0$.
  Thus, in both cases the symbol of $T_0$ has the form $p(\xi)=\Psi(|\xi|^2)$ with $\Psi'(\lambda)>0$ for $\lambda>0$, so the final assertion of Lemma~\ref{lem:generalized-ishida-wada} is applicable.

  Let $R\geq1$ and choose a radial function $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d;[0,1])$ such that
  $$
  \chi(x)=0\quad\text{for }|x|\leq R,
  \qquad
  \chi(x)=1\quad\text{for }|x|\geq2R,
  $$
  Set
  $$
  U^{L}(x) := \chi(x)\frac{\kappa}{|x|^\alpha},
  \qquad
  U^{R}(x) := (1-\chi(x))\frac{\kappa}{|x|^\alpha}.
  $$
  Then $U^{L}\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and, with $\varepsilon_{\rm s}:=\operatorname{sgn}(\kappa)$, there are $c,C>0$ such that
  $$
  c\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha} \leq \varepsilon_{\rm s}U^{L}(x) \leq C\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha}, \quad |x|\geq2R.
  $$
  Thus, the long-range exponent in Lemma~\ref{lem:generalized-ishida-wada} is $\gamma=\alpha\leq1$. Moreover, $U^{R}$ is supported in $B(0,2R)$ and $|U^{R}(x)| \lesssim 1+|x|^{-\alpha}$. Since $\alpha<d$, Lemma~\ref{lem:generalized-ishida-wada} yields the existence of a nonzero $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with $\hat\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\})$, such that, with $\varphi_t:=\mathrm{e}^{-itT_0}\varphi$, we have $\|U^{R}\varphi_t\|_2 \lesssim_N t^{-N}$ for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$.

  Let us also verify the Duhamel formula \eqref{eq:IW-Duhamel}. The function $\hat\varphi_t$ has the same compact support as $\hat\varphi$, and hence $\varphi_t\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $T_0\varphi_t\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Furthermore, $U\varphi_t = U^{L}\varphi_t + U^{R}\varphi_t \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$.
  Since $T_\kappa$ is defined by the corresponding semibounded quadratic form,
  we have $\varphi_t\in\mathcal{D}(T_\kappa)$ and $T_\kappa\varphi_t = T_0\varphi_t-U\varphi_t$. As $t\mapsto U\varphi_t$ is locally continuous in $L^2$,
  $$
  \frac{d}{dt} \left(\mathrm{e}^{itT_\kappa}\mathrm{e}^{-itT_0}\varphi\right)
  = -i\mathrm{e}^{itT_\kappa}U\mathrm{e}^{-itT_0}\varphi
  $$
  for sufficiently large $t$, and integration yields the Duhamel formula \eqref{eq:IW-Duhamel}.

  All assumptions of that lemma are therefore satisfied, and we conclude that $W(T_\kappa,T_0)$ does not exist. Thus, taking $T_0=L_0$ proves Theorem~\ref{asympcomplhardy}(2), while taking $T_0=C_0$ proves Corollary~\ref{cor:massiverelativisticnonexistence}(1).

body_md:
Again, we treat the homogeneous and massive kinetic energies simultaneously.
  Let
  $$
  T_0 =
  \begin{cases}
    L_0 = (-\Delta)^{\alpha/2},\\
    C_0 = C_0(-\Delta).
  \end{cases}
  $$
  Set
  $$
  U(x) := \frac{\kappa}{|x|^\alpha}+V^L(x),
  \qquad
  H := T_0-U.
  $$
  Thus,
  $$
  H =
  \begin{cases}
    L_\kappa-V^L,\\
    C_\kappa-V^L.
  \end{cases}
  $$
  As in the preceding proof, the Fourier symbol of $T_0$ is of the form
  $$
  p(\xi) = \Psi(|\xi|^2),
  \qquad
  \Psi'(\lambda)>0,
  \quad \lambda>0.
  $$
  Hence, Lemma~\ref{lem:generalized-ishida-wada} is applicable.
  We first determine the leading long-range behavior of $U$.

  \smallskip
  \noindent
  {\bf Case 1: $\rho_L<\alpha$.}
  In this case, $|x|^{-\alpha} = o(\langle x\rangle^{-\rho_L})$ as $|x|\to\infty$.
  Let $\varepsilon_L\in\{-1,1\}$ denote the sign of $V^L$, so that by \eqref{ass1} or \eqref{ass2},
  $$
  K_1\langle x\rangle^{-\rho_L} \leq \varepsilon_LV^L(x) \leq K_2\langle x\rangle^{-\rho_L}.
  $$
  Hence, after increasing $R>0$ if necessary,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:nonexistence-total-leading-rho}
    c\langle x\rangle^{-\rho_L} \leq \varepsilon_L U(x) \leq C\langle x\rangle^{-\rho_L}, \quad |x|\geq R.
  \end{align}
  Thus, the leading exponent is $\gamma=\rho_L$.

  \smallskip
  \noindent
  {\bf Case 2: $\rho_L>\alpha$.}
  If $\kappa\neq0$, then $\langle x\rangle^{-\rho_L} = o(|x|^{-\alpha})$, and hence, after increasing $R$,
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:nonexistence-total-leading-alpha}
    c\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha} \leq \operatorname{sgn}(\kappa)U(x) \leq C\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha}, \quad |x|\geq R.
  \end{align}
  Thus, $\gamma=\alpha$. Notice that $\alpha<\rho_L\leq1$, and therefore $\gamma=\alpha<1$.

  If $\kappa=0$, then $U=V^L$, and the long-range assumptions directly give
  $$
  c\langle x\rangle^{-\rho_L} \leq \varepsilon_LU(x) \leq C\langle x\rangle^{-\rho_L}
  $$
  for all $x$, so that $\gamma=\rho_L\leq1$.

  \smallskip
  \noindent
  {\bf Case 3: $\rho_L=\alpha$.}
  Here the two contributions have the same order and may cancel. However, by assumption there exist $\varepsilon_{\rm s}\in\{-1,1\}$, $c>0$, and $R>0$ such that
  \begin{align*}
    \varepsilon_{\rm s} \left(\frac{\kappa}{|x|^\alpha}+V^L(x)\right)
    \geq c\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha}, \quad |x|\geq R.
  \end{align*}
  The assumptions on $V^L$ also give the corresponding upper bound
  $$
  |U(x)| \lesssim \langle x\rangle^{-\alpha}, \quad |x|\geq R.
  $$
  Thus, $\gamma=\alpha=\rho_L\leq1$.

  \smallskip
  In all three cases, we have found $0<\gamma\leq1$, $\varepsilon_{\rm s}\in\{-1,1\}$, and $c,C,R>0$ such that
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:nonexistence-total-tail}
    c\langle x\rangle^{-\gamma} \leq \varepsilon_{\rm s}U(x),
    \qquad
    |U(x)| \leq C\langle x\rangle^{-\gamma}, \quad |x|\geq R.
  \end{align}
  Choose a radial cutoff $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d;[0,1])$ with
  $$
  \chi=0
  \quad\text{on }B(0,R),
  \qquad
  \chi=1
  \quad\text{on }\mathbb{R}^d\setminus B(0,2R),
  $$
  and define
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:nonexistence-UL-UR-cutoff}
    U^{L} := \chi U,
    \qquad
    U^{R} := (1-\chi)U.
  \end{align}
  Then, $U^{L}\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and \eqref{eq:nonexistence-total-tail} implies the assumptions \eqref{eq:IW-leading-lower}--\eqref{eq:IW-leading-upper} in Lemma~\ref{lem:generalized-ishida-wada}.
  On the other hand, $\operatorname{supp} U^{R} \subset B(0,2R)$. Since $V^L\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$,
  $$
  |U^{R}(x)| \lesssim 1+|x|^{-\alpha}.
  $$
  Since $\alpha<d$, Lemma~\ref{lem:generalized-ishida-wada} provides a nonzero $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with $\hat\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\})$ such that, with $\varphi_t:=\mathrm{e}^{-itT_0}\varphi$, we have $\|U^{R}\varphi_t\|_2 \lesssim_N t^{-N}$ for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$.

  The Duhamel formula \eqref{eq:IW-Duhamel} is verified exactly as in the previous subsection.
  Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:generalized-ishida-wada}, $W(H,T_0)$ does not exist.
  For $T_0=L_0$, this proves $W(L_\kappa-V^L,L_0)$ does not exist.
  For $T_0=C_0$, it proves $W(C_\kappa-V^L,C_0)$ does not exist.

Assume $\alpha>1$. We again treat both kinetic energies simultaneously. Set
  $$
  H_0 =
  \begin{cases}
    L_0, \\
    C_0,
  \end{cases}
  \qquad
  H_1 =
  \begin{cases}
    L_\kappa, \\
    C_\kappa,
  \end{cases}
  \qquad
  H_2:=H_1-V^L.
  $$
  By Theorem~\ref{asympcomplhardy}(1), respectively Corollary~\ref{cor:massiverelativisticexistence}(1), the wave operator
  $$
  W_{10}:=W(H_1,H_0)
  $$
  exists and is asymptotically complete. Thus, $\operatorname{ran} W_{10} = \mathcal{H}_{\rm ac}(H_1)$.
  Since $0<\rho_L\leq1<\alpha$, we have, by Theorem~\ref{asympcomplhardyplusperturbationnonexistence}(\ref{asympcomplhardyplusperturbation:nonexistencefree}) and Corollary~\ref{cor:massiverelativisticnonexistence}(2) (proved in the previous subsection), that $W(H_2,H_0)$ does not exist.

  Suppose, contrary to the claim, that the relative wave operator
  \begin{align}
    \label{eq:relative-wave-assume}
    W_{21} := \operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\infty} \mathrm{e}^{itH_2}\mathrm{e}^{-itH_1}P_{\rm ac}(H_1)
  \end{align}
  exists. Then, by the chain rule for wave operators, $W_{20}$ exists; this is a contradiction.
  Thus, taking $(H_0,H_1,H_2) = (L_0,L_\kappa,L_\kappa-V^L)$ proves $W(L_\kappa-V^L,L_\kappa)$ does not exist.
  Taking $(H_0,H_1,H_2) = (C_0,C_\kappa,C_\kappa-V^L)$ proves $W(C_\kappa-V^L,C_\kappa)$ does not exist.

body_md:
Applying Cauchy's formula, for every $t>0$ and $k\in \mathbb{N}$,
  $$
  H^k \mathrm{e}^{-tH} = \frac{(-1)^kk!}{2\pi i}\int_{|\xi-t|=\eta t} \mathrm{e}^{-\xi H}\frac{d\xi}{(\xi-t)^{k+1}},
  $$
  where $\eta>0$ is small enough so that $\{\xi: |\xi-t|=\eta t\}\subset \mathbb{C}_{\tilde\varepsilon\pi/4}$ with $\tilde \varepsilon = \frac{\varepsilon}{d+\alpha}$, and the integral does not depend on the choice of $\eta$. Thus, by Proposition \ref{heatkernelestimates-halfplane} and $|\xi|\simeq |\xi-t|\simeq t$,
  \begin{align*}
    |p_{t,k}(x,y)|
    & \leq C_{k,\tilde\varepsilon} \left(1\wedge\frac{|x|}{t^{1/\alpha}}\right)^{-\sigma} \left(1\wedge\frac{|y|}{t^{1/\alpha}}\right)^{-\sigma}t^{-(k+d/\alpha)} \left(\frac{t^{1/\alpha}+|x-y|}{t^{1/\alpha}}\right)^{-(d+\alpha)(1-\tilde\varepsilon)} \\
    & \leq C_{k,\varepsilon} \left(1\wedge\frac{|x|}{t^{1/\alpha}}\right)^{-\sigma} \left(1\wedge\frac{|y|}{t^{1/\alpha}}\right)^{-\sigma} t^{-(k+d/\alpha)} \left(\frac{t^{1/\alpha}+|x-y|}{t^{1/\alpha}}\right)^{-(d+\alpha-\varepsilon)}
  \end{align*}
  holds for all $x,y\in {\mathbb{R}^d}$ and $t>0$.
